newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich provides ethical relief for Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich provides ethical relief for Clinton.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Fiery Republican Newt Gingrich's re-election as speaker of the House of Representatives could help President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party weather their own ethical problems.
Just when Clinton and the Democrats were braced for months of difficult investigations, Gingrich came over the hill like the U.S. cavalry galloping to the rescue.

Gingrich, re-elected as speaker on Tuesday despite acknowledging ethical violations, will continue to serve as the most unpopular Republican in the nation and a highly visible and convenient target for Democratic attacks.

He faces further investigation by the House Ethics Committee, the Internal Revenue Service and possibly other agencies. He has already admitted to bringing discredit to the House by not doing enough to prevent use of tax-exempt donations for a college course that critics say was for partisan purposes and to unintentionally giving false information to investigators.

The Gingrich investigations will provide a counterweight for Clinton and the Democrats, who face their own ethical inquiries over questionable fundraising practices. Clinton also has to deal with the long-running Whitewater scandals while the Supreme Court next week hears arguments over whether former Arkansas state employee Paula Jones can proceed with a civil suit against Clinton alleging sexual harassment in 1991 when he was governor.

American University political scientist Allan Lichtman said a weakened Gingrich badly needed to restore his tarnished public image. The best way of accomplishing that might be to work with Clinton to pass bipartisan legislation.
"This is the best of all outcomes for the Democrats. They now get to deal with a speaker with a stain on his record, which will help deflect the charges against Clinton," he said.

Representative Linda Smith of Washington state, one of a handful of Republicans who refused to support Gingrich, said the speaker and his party now faced a painful future. "I call it death by a thousand cuts -- half of them self-inflicted and half of them by the piranhas of the Democrats and the media," she said.
Although Democrats pushed hard for Gingrich's defeat, many were privately elated at the outcome of the vote, in which Gingrich received only 216 of the 435 House votes.
"It's a great gift for the president and for our party," said one Democratic operative who asked not to be named.

Representative Scott Klug, a Republican from Wisconsin who had argued that the vote for speaker should be delayed until the status of the charges against Gingrich became clearer, predicted the Democrats would drag out the investigation as long as possible.
"Part of the problem and complicates this whole situation is the fact that clearly the Democrats would like to string this along as long as they could," he said.
Democrats were able to push politically vulnerable Republicans to the wall and get most of them on the record voting for Gingrich.

"It certainly doesn't hurt the Democrats to have a tarnished speaker elected. But I think it hurts the country, and I know it hurts the Congress," Democratic Representative Charles Rangel of New York said.

A rash of polls over the weekend found a substantial majority of Americans and a narrow majority of Republicans thought Gingrich should have stepped down as speaker. In one Gallup poll, which asked respondents who had higher moral standards -- Gingrich or Clinton -- 52 percent said Clinton and 27 percent said Gingrich.
Conservative magazine editor Bill Kristol, who had urged fellow Republicans to vote for Gingrich, said they could always dump him later if he proved too great a liability.

"Six months from now, if Newt Gingrich is a very damaged leader of the Republican Party, it is perfectly appropriate for the Republican caucus to consider electing a new leader as leader of the party and as speaker of the House," he said.
